articles.title: International Society of Biometeorology Celebrates 70 Years of Advancing Science on Weather, Climate and Life
articles.author: Editorial team
articles.content:
The International Society of Biometeorology (ISB) is celebrating its 70th anniversary in 2026, marking seven decades of international scientific cooperation dedicated to understanding how weather, climate and atmospheric conditions influence living organisms. Founded in Paris on 29 August 1956, the society continues to connect researchers working across meteorology, climatology, biology, ecology, physiology and environmental health.

The anniversary year has been marked by the 24th International Congress of Biometeorology (ICB2026), held from 13 to 16 July at the University of Novi Sad in Serbia. The congress brought together more than 200 participants from 40 countries under the theme Biometeorology: Addressing 21st Century Global Climate Issues and Perspectives of Living Beings and Places.

According to the European Meteorological Society (EMS), the congress provided an international forum for scientific exchange on the effects of atmospheric conditions on humans, animals, plants and ecosystems.

Seven Decades of International Scientific Cooperation

The ISB was established to bring together scientists whose work examined the relationships between the physical environment and living systems. Its founding helped create a common international platform for exchanging research and developing biometeorology as an interdisciplinary scientific field.

Today, the society promotes research and the dissemination of knowledge about the relationships between meteorological factors, physical and chemical environmental processes, and living organisms. Its international membership encompasses researchers from a wide range of scientific disciplines.

Biometeorology has applications extending well beyond weather forecasting. It helps explain how heat and cold affect human physiology, how atmospheric conditions influence plant development, how animals respond to environmental extremes and how climate variability affects ecosystems.

The field has become increasingly relevant as societies face rising temperatures, more frequent episodes of extreme heat in many regions and growing concerns about the effects of climate change on human health and the natural environment.

Major Research Themes at ICB2026

The International Congress of Biometeorology in Novi Sad brought together specialists to discuss scientific challenges affecting living organisms and the places in which they live.

According to the EMS report on the congress, sessions organised by ISB commissions and study groups addressed heatwave impacts, variations in air masses, urban climate adaptation, changes in phenological phases, and the effects of extreme weather on agriculture, ecosystems and tourism.

One highlighted contribution examined how the cooling performance of different tree species varies with their growth stage and planting density. Research of this kind can contribute to the planning of urban green spaces and help cities evaluate how vegetation may reduce heat exposure.

The congress also featured scientific awards recognising research published in peer-reviewed journals. These awards illustrated the society's role in supporting scientific quality and encouraging the exchange of new findings among researchers.

A further outcome of the congress was the preparation of special journal collections intended to make selected research contributions available to the wider scientific community.

Human Biometeorology and the Challenge of Extreme Heat

Human biometeorology is one of the most important areas of the discipline. It investigates how environmental conditions influence human thermal comfort, physiological responses and health.

Air temperature alone cannot fully describe the thermal stress experienced by a person outdoors. Humidity, wind speed, solar radiation, exposure duration and individual characteristics all influence the body's ability to regulate its internal temperature.

Biometeorological indices such as the Universal Thermal Climate Index help researchers assess the combined effects of environmental conditions on human thermal stress. Such information can support heat-health warning systems, urban planning and measures designed to protect vulnerable populations.

Older adults, young children, outdoor workers and people with certain existing health conditions may be particularly vulnerable during periods of extreme heat. By bringing meteorological and health research together, biometeorology can help improve understanding of these risks and support more effective preventive action.

The ISB's interdisciplinary approach is particularly valuable in this area because reliable assessment of heat-related health risks requires expertise in atmospheric science, physiology, epidemiology and public health.

Cooperation with the European Meteorological Society

International cooperation was also strengthened during the anniversary year. On 24 September 2026, the European Meteorological Society announced that it had extended its memorandum of understanding with the ISB for another five years.

The agreement was signed by EMS President Liz Bentley and ISB President Tanja Cegnar during the EMS Annual Meeting 2026 in Utrecht, the Netherlands.

According to the EMS announcement, the renewed agreement will help the organisations coordinate their major conferences, avoiding scheduling conflicts and enabling members to benefit from both EMS Annual Meetings and the International Congress of Biometeorology.

The continuation of this partnership is important for maintaining links between biometeorology and the broader European meteorological community. It also creates opportunities for researchers to exchange knowledge and strengthen cooperation across scientific disciplines.

The Future of Biometeorology

As climate change alters environmental conditions in many parts of the world, the scientific questions addressed by biometeorology are becoming increasingly important.

Researchers need to understand how organisms respond to changing temperatures, how urban environments influence human exposure to heat, how agricultural systems react to weather extremes and how environmental changes affect the timing of biological processes.

Answering these questions requires international observations, reliable datasets, consistent research methods and cooperation between scientists working in different disciplines and geographical regions.

The International Society of Biometeorology provides a forum for this exchange. Its 70th anniversary is an opportunity to recognise the development of biometeorology since 1956 and to highlight the importance of research connecting the atmosphere with human health, biological systems and the environment.

As the discipline continues to develop, its contribution will extend beyond understanding weather and climate. It will also help societies interpret environmental risks, improve adaptation strategies and make better-informed decisions to protect people and ecosystems.

articles.title: New Scientific Paper Calls for Greater Accuracy in the Use of Biometeorological Indices
articles.author: Editorial team
articles.content:
A scientific paper published in the International Journal of Biometeorology on 22 September 2026 calls for more careful selection and reporting of biometeorological indices used to assess environmental conditions and their effects on human activities. The paper highlights an important methodological challenge: although these indices have become easier to calculate, their results may be misleading when they are applied without considering the location, purpose and assumptions for which they were developed.

The article, written by Jennifer M. Fitchett of the University of the Witwatersrand in South Africa, proposes a conceptual framework for evaluating the applicability, suitability and validity of biometeorological indices before they are used in research or to inform policy.

Its central message is that a numerical result is only useful when the method producing it is appropriate for the question being investigated.

What Are Biometeorological Indices?

Biometeorological indices combine meteorological measurements into a value or category that helps describe how environmental conditions may affect people, animals, plants or particular activities.

In human biometeorology, indices are frequently used to assess thermal comfort and heat or cold stress. Depending on the method, calculations may incorporate air temperature, humidity, wind speed, solar radiation and other environmental variables.

Examples include the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI), which is used to assess outdoor thermal stress, and the Physiologically Equivalent Temperature (PET), which expresses outdoor thermal conditions in terms of an equivalent temperature under a defined reference environment.

Different indices have different mathematical structures, assumptions and intended applications. Some are designed primarily for human thermal comfort, while others are used to assess climatic suitability for tourism, recreation or particular outdoor activities.

Consequently, two indices applied to the same meteorological observations may produce different classifications. This does not automatically mean that one calculation is incorrect; the difference may reflect the methods' distinct assumptions and intended purposes.

Why Choosing the Right Index Matters

In her paper, Fitchett explains that the increasing availability of high-quality meteorological datasets and computing tools has made it possible to calculate biometeorological indices rapidly across large geographical areas and long periods.

This development has expanded research opportunities, but it has also created a risk: researchers may apply an index outside the environmental conditions, geographical settings or activities for which its suitability has been established.

An index that performs adequately in one climatic region may not represent people's thermal experiences equally well in another. Differences in acclimatisation, local building characteristics, exposure patterns and other environmental factors can influence how people experience the same measured conditions.

The problem becomes particularly important when index results are used to guide practical decisions. If an assessment incorrectly characterises heat stress or climatic suitability, the resulting recommendations for urban planning, tourism, outdoor work or climate adaptation may be inappropriate.

The paper therefore argues for a more systematic evaluation of the methods used before interpreting their results.

A Framework Based on Applicability, Suitability and Validity

Fitchett's proposed framework identifies three central considerations.

Applicability concerns whether an index is appropriate for the particular research question, population, activity and environmental conditions being examined.

Suitability concerns whether the index's design and assumptions are a good fit for the intended application. Researchers must consider what the index actually measures and whether that measurement addresses the question they want to answer.

Validity concerns whether the index provides a sufficiently reliable representation of the phenomenon under investigation. This may require comparison with observations, relevant empirical evidence or established findings from previous research.

These considerations are related but distinct. An index may be straightforward to calculate and widely used without necessarily being the best choice for a specific location or purpose.

The proposed framework encourages researchers to explain why they selected a particular index and to make its limitations clear when presenting results.

Implications for Heat-Health Research

The recommendations are especially relevant to research into heat-related health risks. During heatwaves, meteorological services and public-health authorities need reliable information about the environmental conditions experienced by people.

An index used to assess outdoor thermal stress can help identify potentially hazardous conditions, compare heat exposure across locations and support the development of warning systems. However, the interpretation of its output must reflect the index's assumptions and the characteristics of the population being studied.

For example, a thermal index calculated for outdoor conditions should not automatically be treated as a complete measure of heat exposure inside buildings. Indoor conditions may be influenced by insulation, ventilation, air conditioning, building materials and the amount of direct solar radiation entering the structure.

Similarly, a thermal stress category should not be interpreted as a direct prediction of an individual's medical outcome. Health risks depend on additional factors, including age, existing health conditions, duration of exposure and access to cooling.

Careful index selection is therefore one part of a broader process that combines meteorological information with relevant physiological, epidemiological and environmental evidence.

Relevance to Climate Adaptation and Urban Planning

Biometeorological indices are increasingly relevant to the assessment of urban heat, the design of public spaces and the planning of climate-resilient cities. Researchers can use them to investigate how trees, shade, surface materials and urban layouts influence thermal conditions experienced by people.

However, the reliability of such assessments depends partly on whether the chosen index captures the effects that matter for the particular question. A method intended to assess human thermal comfort may not, by itself, provide a complete assessment of building energy demand, public-health risk or the suitability of a destination for tourism.

The paper's framework offers a way to improve transparency by encouraging researchers to justify their methods, recognise their limitations and avoid treating all biometeorological indices as interchangeable.

For policymakers, this is an important distinction. Numerical maps and risk categories can appear authoritative, but their usefulness depends on the quality of the underlying measurements, the appropriateness of the calculation method and the interpretation of the results.

A Call for More Transparent Biometeorological Research

The paper does not argue that biometeorological indices should be abandoned. Instead, it calls for more critical and consistent engagement with the methods that researchers use.

As climate datasets become increasingly detailed and computational tools make large-scale analysis easier, the scientific challenge is no longer limited to calculating an index. Researchers must also demonstrate that the chosen method is suitable for the environmental conditions, population and decisions to which it is being applied.

This is particularly important when research informs heat-health warnings, urban adaptation strategies or recommendations intended to protect vulnerable people.

Fitchett's contribution provides a conceptual basis for making those choices more explicit. Its wider significance lies in a fundamental principle of applied science: more data and more calculations do not automatically produce better decisions. Scientific results become more reliable when methods are carefully selected, appropriately validated and interpreted within their limitations.

Scientific source

Fitchett, J. M. (2026). “Critical engagement on the selection and reporting of biometeorological indices.” International Journal of Biometeorology, volume 70, article 261. Published online on 22 September 2026.

Full text: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00484-026-03328-9

DOI: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00484-026-03328-9

Editorial note: This article summarises the arguments and conceptual framework presented in Fitchett's published paper. The three-part framework is the author's proposed approach; it should not be described as a newly adopted international standard or a mandatory protocol for all biometeorological research.

articles.title: Utrecht Workshop Highlights the Growing Role of Biometeorology in Protecting Human Health
articles.author: Editorial team
articles.content:
Utrecht, The Netherlands

A specialist workshop held in Utrecht on 10 September 2026 brought together experts from meteorology, climate science and public health to examine how atmospheric conditions affect human health and how scientific knowledge can be translated into practical protection measures.

The workshop, titled Living with the Elements: Weather, Climate, and Human Health, formed part of the European Meteorological Society's (EMS) Annual Meeting 2026, held in Utrecht and online from 6 to 11 September. Hosted at the Jaarbeurs Convention Centre, the event focused on human biometeorology, heat-health warning systems, environmental health risks and the communication of scientific information to decision-makers and the public.

The workshop was convened by Tanja Cegnar of the International Society of Biometeorology and Aleksandra Kazmierczak of the European Environment Agency's European Climate and Health Observatory. It was organised in cooperation with the Solco W. Tromp Foundation, the International Society of Biometeorology, the European Climate and Health Observatory, the European Meteorological Society, the Slovenian Meteorological Society and the Slovenian Environment Agency (ARSO).

Connecting Weather, Climate and Human Health

Biometeorology examines the interactions between atmospheric conditions and living organisms. Human biometeorology focuses particularly on how weather and climate influence human physiology, thermal comfort, health and everyday activities.

The Utrecht workshop addressed an increasingly important challenge: turning meteorological and climate information into practical knowledge that can help protect people from environmental hazards.

Temperature alone does not fully describe the conditions experienced by the human body. Humidity, wind speed, solar radiation and the duration of exposure can all influence thermal stress. These factors are particularly important during heatwaves, when the body may struggle to release excess heat, especially if hot conditions continue overnight.

The workshop explored how better integration of meteorological observations, health information and epidemiological modelling can improve understanding of weather-related health risks and support more effective prevention.

Heat-Health Warning Systems and Early Action

One of the workshop's principal themes was the development and application of heat-health warning systems. These systems combine weather forecasts with information about potential health impacts, helping public authorities and healthcare services prepare for periods of dangerous heat.

Reliable warnings can support decisions about outdoor work, healthcare preparedness, public communication and the protection of vulnerable groups. Older adults, young children, people with chronic illnesses and outdoor workers may face particular risks during extreme heat.

Participants also examined the role of data infrastructure, including the European Climate and Health Observatory and the Copernicus Health Hub, in connecting environmental information with the needs of the health sector.

The wider objective is to make climate and weather information more useful to those responsible for protecting public health, rather than treating meteorological forecasts and health planning as separate activities.

Beyond Heat: Air Pollution, Infectious Diseases and Drought

The workshop's scope extended beyond thermal stress. Its programme also addressed relationships between atmospheric conditions and air pollution, hospital admissions, weather-sensitive infectious diseases and drought-related vulnerabilities.

Air pollution, for example, can affect respiratory and cardiovascular health, while weather conditions influence the formation, transport and dispersion of certain pollutants. Changes in temperature and rainfall can also alter environmental conditions relevant to some infectious diseases.

These relationships are complex, and the health effects of any particular weather event depend on multiple factors. Biometeorological research therefore relies on meteorological observations, health data and appropriate scientific methods to distinguish associations from causal relationships.

By bringing together specialists from different disciplines, the workshop aimed to encourage closer collaboration and improve the practical application of research findings.

Science Communication and Health Equity

Another important topic was the unequal distribution of environmental health risks. Exposure to heat and other climate-related hazards can vary substantially according to housing quality, occupation, access to healthcare, income and the availability of cooling or green spaces.

Communicating risks clearly is essential. Warnings must be scientifically sound, understandable and relevant to the people expected to act on them. The workshop therefore considered how new technologies, artificial intelligence, urban heat modelling and public-health frameworks can support more effective communication.

The discussions also highlighted the importance of translating scientific knowledge into recommendations that public authorities, communities and individuals can use when preparing for hazardous weather conditions.

International Cooperation for a Changing Climate

The Utrecht workshop was part of the broader EMS Annual Meeting 2026, whose central theme was Delta Climate in Europe: Weather, Water, and Warnings. The meeting addressed challenges associated with climate change, atmospheric science, water management, early warnings and societal preparedness.

The biometeorology workshop contributed a specific human-health perspective to these wider discussions. Its emphasis on cooperation between meteorological services, public-health institutions and research organisations reflects the growing importance of interdisciplinary approaches to climate adaptation.

As extreme heat, air pollution and other environmental hazards continue to pose challenges to communities worldwide, biometeorology provides a scientific framework for understanding how atmospheric conditions affect human well-being.

The Utrecht meeting highlighted the value of connecting research, operational forecasting and public-health action. Strengthening these links can help improve warning systems, guide adaptation measures and support more informed decisions in a changing climate.

Sources

It summarises the workshop's stated aims and themes and does not attribute unverified quotations, decisions or research findings to individual participants.

articles.title: ‘Heat Storms’: A New Way to Understand the Growing Global Threat of Extreme Heat
articles.author: Editorial team
articles.content:
LONDON — A new international investigation published by Reuters on 20 October 2026 has highlighted the growing scale and persistence of extreme heat events around the world. The analysis introduces the term heat storms to describe exceptionally large heatwaves that extend across substantial portions of the Earth's surface, sometimes lasting for months.

The investigation analysed hourly temperature data from more than one million grid cells covering the globe, examining conditions dating back to 1960. Its findings suggest that extreme heat events have changed considerably over the past six decades, becoming more widespread and accounting for a growing proportion of unusually hot days.


The research offers a new perspective on a problem of major importance to biometeorology: how prolonged exposure to abnormal atmospheric conditions affects human health, animal life, ecosystems and the environments in which people live.

From Heatwaves to Continental-Scale Events

Reuters developed the term heat storm for its investigation, defining these events as heatwaves that last at least five consecutive days and cover at least 1% of the Earth's surface at their peak. This is a threshold established for the investigation, rather than a universally accepted scientific definition.

According to the analysis, approximately five such events were active annually during the 1960s, compared with an average of around 102 per year during the current decade. The investigation also found that heat storms accounted for nearly 43% of unusually hot days during the 2020s, compared with approximately 3% in the 1960s.

One of the largest events identified by the investigation, named Heat Storm Vera by Reuters, lasted 367 days during 2023–2024 and covered nearly 85% of the globe at its peak. The investigation documents how prolonged heat affected communities, wildlife, agriculture and infrastructure in different parts of the world.

These findings illustrate why the geographical extent and duration of extreme heat deserve as much attention as individual temperature records. A heatwave affecting several countries simultaneously can place pressure on electricity supplies, water resources, healthcare services and food production across large regions.

Why Prolonged Heat Matters to Biometeorology

Biometeorology studies the relationships between atmospheric conditions and living organisms. Human biometeorology, in particular, examines how temperature, humidity, wind and radiation influence the human body's thermal balance and physiological responses.

During hot weather, the human body relies heavily on sweating and the evaporation of moisture from the skin to release excess heat. High humidity can reduce the effectiveness of this cooling mechanism, while direct sunlight increases the body's heat load. When hot conditions persist for several days, the opportunity for physiological recovery may become limited, particularly if nighttime temperatures remain elevated.

Prolonged heat exposure can contribute to dehydration, heat exhaustion and heatstroke. It can also aggravate existing cardiovascular and respiratory conditions. Older people, young children, outdoor workers and people without access to adequately cooled buildings may face increased risks.

The consequences extend beyond human health. The Reuters investigation describes extreme heat affecting freshwater ecosystems, wildlife and agricultural production. During the 2023–2024 event, unusually high temperatures in parts of the Amazon contributed to severe stress on aquatic ecosystems, including the mass mortality of river dolphins in Lake Tefé.

Such examples demonstrate that heat should not be assessed solely by the maximum temperature recorded at a weather station. Its duration, geographical coverage, humidity, local environmental conditions and the sensitivity of exposed organisms all influence the resulting impacts.

Climate Change and the Expansion of Extreme Heat

The investigation attributes the long-term intensification of extreme heat primarily to human-driven global warming, while also examining the role of natural climate variability, including El Niño.

El Niño is a recurring climate phenomenon associated with unusually warm sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. It influences atmospheric circulation and changes the likelihood of temperature and rainfall extremes in different parts of the world. Its regional effects vary, and it does not produce identical weather conditions everywhere.

In a separate announcement published on 8 October 2026, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) reported that El Niño was strengthening and forecast to influence global temperature and rainfall patterns during October–December 2026. The WMO warned of increased risks of above-average temperatures in many regions, alongside shifts in rainfall that could raise the likelihood of drought in some areas and flooding in others.

The WMO outlook provides a complementary perspective on the climate conditions that can influence heat exposure. However, seasonal forecasts describe probabilities over broad regions; they do not establish that a particular heatwave will occur at a specific location.

The combination of long-term global warming and natural climate variability makes continued monitoring essential for understanding how extreme heat develops and where its impacts may be greatest.

Improving Heat Warnings and Public Protection

For meteorological services, one of the main challenges is translating complex temperature data into useful warnings for the public. Conventional forecasts remain essential, but biometeorological indicators can provide additional information about the conditions experienced by the human body.

The Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI), for example, combines several environmental factors to assess outdoor thermal stress. The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts provides global ERA5-HEAT data that can be used to study how weather conditions affect human thermal comfort and heat exposure over time.

Combining such information with health surveillance, urban planning and emergency preparedness can help authorities identify periods of elevated risk. Possible responses include issuing early warnings, adjusting outdoor working schedules, improving access to shade and cooling, and protecting people who are particularly vulnerable to heat.

Long-lasting heat events also reinforce the importance of urban design. Trees, shaded public spaces, appropriate building design and access to cool indoor environments can reduce exposure in many settings, although the effectiveness of individual measures depends on local climate and infrastructure.

A Changing Challenge for Global Health and the Environment

The Reuters investigation presents a striking picture of how extreme heat events have expanded over recent decades. Its proposed heat storm terminology is intended to make the scale and persistence of these events easier to communicate, although the concept will require further scientific evaluation before it can be treated as a standard meteorological classification.

For biometeorology, the broader message is clear: understanding the effects of extreme heat requires more than measuring air temperature. Scientists must also consider how long the heat lasts, how much territory it affects, how the human body responds and how ecosystems react to prolonged thermal stress.

As the planet continues to warm, reliable meteorological observations, health research and effective early-warning systems will be increasingly important for reducing the impacts of extreme heat on people and the natural environment.
